title: Scalar vs. vector quantity
body: A scalar is described by magnitude only; a vector is described by both magnitude and direction.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.1 "Scalars are quantities described by magnitude only; vectors are quantities described by both magnitude and direction."

title: Scalar and vector kinematic quantities
body: The CED's examples of scalar quantities and of vector quantities.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.3 "Distance and speed are examples of scalar quantities, while position, displacement, velocity, and acceleration are examples of vector quantities."

title: Vector arrow representation
body: A vector is drawn as an arrow whose direction is the vector's direction and whose length is proportional to its magnitude.

items.label: Arrow length
items.meaning: Proportional to the magnitude of the vector

ced_evidence: 1.1.A.2 "Vectors can be visually modeled as arrows with appropriate direction and lengths proportional to their magnitude."

title: Velocity change under constant acceleration (vector form)
body: \vec{v}=\vec{v}_0+\vec{a}t
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.3.i "Relevant equation: v = v0 + at"

title: Vector notation vs. signed components in 1-D
body: Vectors are written with an arrow above the symbol, but vector notation is not required for components along an axis because in one dimension the sign of the component completely describes its direction.
ced_evidence: 1.1.A.3.i and 1.1.A.3.ii "the sign of the component completely describes the direction of that component"

title: 1-D vector sum: opposite directions get opposite signs
body: In a given one-dimensional coordinate system, add vectors as signed values, with opposite directions denoted by opposite signs.
ced_evidence: 1.1.B.1 "opposite directions are denoted by opposite signs"

title: Object model
body: In the object model, the object's size, shape, and internal configuration are ignored, so it may be treated as a single point with extensive properties such as mass and charge.
ced_evidence: 1.2.A.1 "size, shape, and internal configuration are ignored"

title: Displacement
body: \Delta x = x - x_0
ced_evidence: 1.2.A.2 "Displacement is the change in an object's position."

title: Average velocity
body: \vec{v}_{avg}=\frac{\Delta \vec{x}}{\Delta t}
ced_evidence: 1.2.B.2 "Average velocity is the displacement of an object divided by the interval of time"

title: Average acceleration
body: \vec{a}_{avg}=\frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}
ced_evidence: 1.2.B.3 "Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the interval of time"

title: Averages use initial and final states
body: Averages of velocity and acceleration are calculated from the initial and final states of an object over an interval of time.
ced_evidence: 1.2.B.1 "calculated considering the initial and final states of an object over an interval of time"

title: Accelerating object
body: An object is accelerating if the magnitude and/or direction of its velocity is changing.
caution: Speeding up, slowing down, and changing direction all count as accelerating; do not say acceleration is negative only when an object slows down, since the sign depends on the chosen axis direction.
ced_evidence: 1.2.B.4 "magnitude and/or direction of the object's velocity are changing"

title: Instantaneous velocity and acceleration
body: Average velocity or average acceleration calculated over a very small time interval is very close to the instantaneous velocity or instantaneous acceleration.
ced_evidence: 1.2.B.5 "over a very small time interval yields a value that is very close to the instantaneous velocity"

title: Representations of motion
body: The CED's ways to represent an object's motion.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.1 "motion diagrams, figures, graphs, equations, and narrative descriptions"

title: Kinematic equation: velocity vs. time (constant acceleration)
body: v_x = v_{x0} + a_x t
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.2 "v x = v x0 + ax t"

title: Kinematic equation: position vs. time (constant acceleration)
body: x = x_0 + v_{x0}t + \tfrac{1}{2}a_x t^2

title: Kinematic equation: velocity vs. position (constant acceleration)
Kinematic equations apply to constant acceleration, in any single dimension
body: The three kinematic equations describe constant-acceleration motion and, though written for x, can be used along any single dimension as appropriate.
caution: Nonuniform acceleration is analyzed only qualitatively (sketching graphs and discussing), never with these equations.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.2 "these equations can be used in any single dimension"; Boundary Statement "does not expect students to quantitatively analyze nonuniform acceleration"

title: Free-fall acceleration near Earth's surface
body: g \approx 10\ \text{m/s}^2 \text{ (downward, constant)}
caution: Using 9.8 or 9.81 m/s^2 is also acceptable and is not penalized.
ced_evidence: 1.3.A.3 "vertical acceleration caused by the force of gravity is downward, constant"; Boundary Statement g = 10 m/s^2

title: Slope and area relationships on motion graphs
body: How position, velocity, and acceleration graphs relate to each other.

items.label: Slope of tangent on x vs. t
Slope of tangent on v vs. t
Area under a vs. t
items.meaning: Change in velocity during the interval

ced_evidence: 1.3.A.4.i-iv "slope of a line tangent to a point"; "area under the curve"

title: Reference frame determines measured direction and magnitude
body: The choice of reference frame determines the direction and magnitude of quantities measured by an observer in that frame.
ced_evidence: 1.4.A.1 "The choice of reference frame will determine the direction and magnitude of quantities"

title: Relative velocity by 1-D vector addition or subtraction
body: An observed velocity combines the object's velocity and the velocity of the observer's frame by adding or subtracting vectors, restricted to one dimension in AP Physics 1.
caution: Two-dimensional relative-velocity problems are out of scope.
ced_evidence: 1.4.B.2.i "involves the addition or subtraction of vectors"; Boundary Statement "restricted to motion along one dimension"

title: Acceleration is the same in all inertial frames
body: The acceleration of any object is the same as measured from all inertial reference frames, whereas velocity depends on the observer's frame.
ced_evidence: 1.4.B.2.ii "acceleration of any object is the same as measured from all inertial reference frames"

title: Assume an inertial frame unless told otherwise
body: Unless otherwise stated, the frame of reference of any problem may be assumed to be inertial.
ced_evidence: Boundary Statement "may be assumed to be inertial"

title: Vectors resolve into perpendicular components
body: A vector can be modeled as the resultant of two perpendicular components, found by resolving it along a chosen coordinate system.
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.1 "resultant of two perpendicular components"; 1.5.A.2 "using a chosen coordinate system"

title: Sine of angle (a opposite, c hypotenuse)
body: \sin\theta = \frac{a}{c}
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.3 "Relevant equations: sin"

hooks.when_to_use: When recalling which side ratio goes with sin, cos, and tan while resolving a vector.
hooks.caution: The mnemonic is not the answer; write the actual ratios with the sides labeled relative to the angle used.

title: Cosine of angle (b adjacent, c hypotenuse)
body: \cos\theta = \frac{b}{c}
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.3 "Relevant equations: cos"

hooks.when_to_use: When recalling which side ratio goes with sin, cos, and tan while resolving a vector.
hooks.caution: The mnemonic is not the answer; write the actual ratios with the sides labeled relative to the angle used.

title: Tangent of angle (a opposite, b adjacent)
body: \tan\theta = \frac{a}{b}
ced_evidence: 1.5.A.3 "Relevant equations: tan"

hooks.when_to_use: When recalling which side ratio goes with sin, cos, and tan while resolving a vector.
hooks.caution: The mnemonic is not the answer; write the actual ratios with the sides labeled relative to the angle used.

title: Pythagorean relationship for vector components
Analyze 2-D motion by separating components
body: Motion in two dimensions can be analyzed with one-dimensional kinematic relationships applied to each component separately.
ced_evidence: 1.5.B.1 "if the motion is separated into components"

title: Projectile motion
body: Projectile motion is a special case of two-dimensional motion with zero acceleration in one dimension and constant, nonzero acceleration in the second dimension.
ced_evidence: 1.5.B.2 "zero acceleration in one dimension and constant, nonzero acceleration in the second dimension"
